title: Brain Immune Cells, Not Plaques, Drive Sleep Loss in Alzheimer's — and the Damage Is Reversible
excerpt: University of Kentucky researchers restored two hours of daily sleep in Alzheimer's mouse models by depleting overactive microglia, without removing a single amyloid plaque from the brain.
body:
• University of Kentucky researchers discovered that microglia — the brain's immune cells — are the primary drivers of sleep loss in Alzheimer's disease, not the amyloid plaques themselves.
  • By temporarily depleting 87% of microglia using a cancer drug called pexidartinib, the team restored more than two hours of sleep per day in mouse models without removing a single amyloid plaque.
  • The study found that Alzheimer's specifically targets NREM (restorative) sleep, while normal aging selectively reduces REM (dreaming) sleep — suggesting the two processes damage different sleep systems.
  • The lab is now exploring whether existing medications like metformin and the anti-seizure drug stiripentol could calm overactive microglia without removing them entirely.

For decades, the prevailing explanation for why Alzheimer's patients lose sleep was straightforward: amyloid plaques — the sticky protein clumps that accumulate in the brain — were either killing neurons or physically disrupting brain circuits. A new study from the University of Kentucky upends that narrative entirely, identifying the brain's own immune system as the real culprit and demonstrating that sleep can be restored without clearing a single plaque.

The Sprinkler Problem

Lead researcher Shannon L. Macauley, an associate professor of physiology at the UK College of Medicine, uses a vivid analogy: imagine a small fire in your kitchen. Before you can put it out with the right tool, the sprinkler system activates and floods your entire house. The fire was contained, but the automatic response destroyed everything.

In Alzheimer's brains, amyloid plaques are the fire. Microglia — the brain's resident immune cells — are the sprinklers. Their job is to detect threats and mount a protective response. But the research, published in Alzheimer's & Dementia in July 2026, shows that this protective response itself becomes the problem.

"We showed that it is not the plaques themselves, or solely dysfunctional neurons, that cause sleep loss but actually microglia. They kick off this elaborate cascade of inflammation, as if the microglia are partying all night, and keeping the brain awake."

— Shannon L. Macauley, Ph.D., University of Kentucky

How the Discovery Was Made

The team, led by first author Nicholas J. Constantino, compared mice genetically predisposed to develop amyloid plaques against normal aging mice at 6 months (when plaques first emerge) and 18 months (late-stage disease). Each mouse was fitted with tiny head mounts to record EEG brain activity and EMG muscle movement, allowing the researchers to track exactly when animals were in deep restorative sleep, dreaming sleep, or awake.

To visualize where immune cells were active, the team used light-sheet microscopy — a technique that makes brain tissue transparent and uses a thin laser to create high-resolution 3D maps. This allowed them to see the entire landscape of plaques and immune cells simultaneously, revealing that microglia expanded across all brain regions, even areas with little or no amyloid buildup.

One finding surprised even the researchers. Constantino expected that sleep disruption would worsen as plaque burden increased. Instead, the disruptions that appeared at 6 months — when plaques first emerged — did not worsen by 18 months, despite plaque levels more than doubling. The initial immune storm, not the ongoing plaque accumulation, was what caused the damage.

Two Hours of Sleep Restored

The breakthrough experiment used pexidartinib (PLX3397), a cancer drug that blocks a survival signal microglia depend on. After 14 days of treatment, 87% of the brain's immune cells were temporarily removed. The result: Alzheimer's mice gained more than two hours of sleep per day. Their NREM sleep bouts — the deep, restorative stage critical for physical repair, learning, and toxin clearance — became longer, giving the brain more opportunities to transition into healthy dreaming sleep.

Crucially, this happened without any change in plaque levels. The inflammatory response, not the plaques triggering it, was a reversible cause of sleep loss that could be treated independently.

Aging vs. Alzheimer's: Different Sleep Targets

The study also clarified a distinction that had been poorly understood. Normal aging selectively reduces REM sleep — the stage where we dream and consolidate memories. Alzheimer's pathology specifically targets NREM sleep, the restorative stage the brain uses for physical repair and clearing daily toxins.

When Alzheimer's patients lose NREM sleep, they lose their brain's primary cleaning cycle. This creates a destructive feedback loop: less cleaning means more toxic buildup, which triggers more immune response, which disrupts more sleep. Breaking that loop — even without addressing plaques directly — could have cascading benefits.

What Comes Next

Removing 87% of microglia is not a viable long-term treatment — these cells serve essential functions beyond their role in Alzheimer's. Macauley's lab is now investigating ways to calm overactive microglia without eliminating them. Two existing medications are under study: metformin, widely used for diabetes, and stiripentol, an anti-seizure drug. Both may be able to reset how microglia metabolize fuel, reducing their hyperactivity without removing them.

The team also identified specific electrical brain signatures that distinguish Alzheimer's from normal aging, suggesting that portable EEG systems could eventually screen for early Alzheimer's changes in home environments — without the expense of brain scans or invasive testing. Macauley envisions doctors at local clinics screening at-risk patients before referring them to specialized centers.

The immediate clinical question is whether this approach translates to humans. If overactive microglia can be calmed in Alzheimer's patients, the potential benefits extend beyond sleep to attention, cognition, and the confusion that makes the disease devastating for patients and families alike. Macauley called the findings "paradigm shifting" — a bold claim, but one backed by data that fundamentally reframes what drives one of Alzheimer's most debilitating symptoms.
nri_angle: Alzheimer's affects millions of families in the Indian diaspora, and the study's focus on affordable, noninvasive biomarkers like portable EEG could have particular relevance for underserved communities.
